details:
**The Importance of Being Earnest**
Wilde's most famous comedy (1895), a farce built on the pun between "earnest" and the name Ernest. Jack Worthing calls himself "Ernest" in London, and his friend Algernon Moncrieff also poses as "Ernest" to woo Jack's ward, Cecily Cardew. Both Cecily and Gwendolen Fairfax insist they can only love a man named Ernest, so both men arrange to be christened by Dr. Chasuble.

**Bunburying**
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Algernon invents a permanently sick friend named Bunbury as an excuse to escape social obligations, such as dinners with his aunt Lady Bracknell. The play opens with his servant Lane preparing cucumber sandwiches for Lady Bracknell's visit, and Algernon eats them all.

**The handbag at Victoria Station**
The revelation in The Importance of Being Earnest that Jack was found as a baby in a handbag in the cloakroom at Victoria Station, where the absent-minded governess Miss Prism had left him by mistake. Lady Bracknell remarks that losing one parent may be a misfortune but "to lose both looks like carelessness," and objects to a man whose origin was a "Terminus." Jack turns out to be Algernon's older brother, and his real name is in fact Ernest.

**Lady Windermere's Fan**
Wilde's 1892 comedy. Lady Margaret Windermere finds payments to the scandalous Mrs. Erlynne in her husband's bank book and suspects an affair, because of his daily visits to her in Curzon Street. She threatens to strike Mrs. Erlynne with her fan, then runs off to Lord Darlington's rooms, where she leaves the fan behind. Mrs. Erlynne, secretly her mother, saves her reputation by claiming the fan is hers, and at the end Mrs. Erlynne is set to marry Lord Augustus Lorton.

**"We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars"**
A line spoken by Lord Darlington in Lady Windermere's Fan. The same play gives Lord Darlington the definition of a cynic as "a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing," in reply to Cecil Graham, and has Dumby say that there are only two tragedies in the world, "not getting what one wants, and getting it."

**"The Ballad of Reading Gaol"**
A long poem Wilde wrote after his release from prison and published in 1898 under his prison number, "C.3.3." Its famous refrain is "Yet each man kills the thing he loves," followed by "The coward does it with a kiss, / The brave man with a sword!" It describes a condemned man who "looked / So wistfully at the day."

**Charles Thomas Wooldridge**
The real Royal Horse Guards trooper, hanged at Reading Gaol in 1896 for murdering his wife, to whom "The Ballad of Reading Gaol" is dedicated. The poem opens "He did not wear his scarlet coat, / For blood and wine are red."

**The Picture of Dorian Gray**
Wilde's only novel (1890/1891). The painter Basil Hallward paints a portrait of the beautiful young Dorian, who falls under the influence of the cynical Lord Henry Wotton and wishes that the picture would age instead of him. The portrait grows old and ugly with each of his sins while he stays young. Dorian murders Basil, and when he finally stabs the painting, he is found dead and withered beside a restored portrait.

**Sibyl Vane**
In Dorian Gray, a young actress who plays Shakespeare's heroines and calls Dorian "Prince Charming." After falling in love, she gives a wooden performance, and Dorian cruelly rejects her, so she kills herself. Her brother James Vane, a sailor, later hunts Dorian for revenge.

**Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray**
A list of aphorisms defending aestheticism, ending "All art is quite useless." It also says that the nineteenth century's dislike of Realism is "the rage of Caliban seeing his own face in a glass," and that there is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book.

**De Profundis**
A long letter Wilde wrote in Reading Gaol to his lover Lord Alfred "Bosie" Douglas. Its title is the Latin opening of Psalm 130 ("Out of the depths"), and it contains the line "Suffering is one very long moment." In it Wilde reproaches Douglas and reflects on his own downfall.

**Lord Alfred Douglas and the trials**
Wilde's relationship with Douglas led Douglas's father, the Marquess of Queensberry, to plan to disrupt the premiere of Earnest with a bouquet of rotten vegetables and to accuse Wilde of homosexuality. Wilde's failed libel suit against Queensberry led to his conviction for "gross indecency." Douglas's poem "Two Loves" coined the phrase "the love that dare not speak its name," and A. E. Housman's "Oh who is that young sinner" was inspired by Wilde's imprisonment.

**Salome**
A one-act tragedy Wilde wrote in French, about the princess who performs the Dance of the Seven Veils for Herod and demands the head of John the Baptist (Jokanaan). It opens with a Page warning the young Syrian not to keep looking at Salome. Herod orders her killed after she kisses the severed head. The Lord Chamberlain banned it from the English stage for showing biblical characters; the English translation, credited to Douglas, was illustrated by Aubrey Beardsley; and Richard Strauss turned it into an opera.

**An Ideal Husband**
Wilde's 1895 play, premiered at the Haymarket Theatre. Sir Robert Chiltern made his fortune by selling a Cabinet secret about Suez Canal shares to Baron Arnheim. Mrs. Cheveley blackmails him into supporting a fraudulent Argentine canal scheme, and Lord Goring foils her with a diamond brooch she once stole. Lady Chiltern learns to forgive her husband for not being perfect.

**Fairy tales: "The Happy Prince" and "The Nightingale and the Rose"**
In "The Happy Prince," a jeweled statue asks a swallow to strip away his rubies, sapphires, and gold leaf for the poor, and the swallow stays with him into winter and dies. In "The Nightingale and the Rose," a nightingale presses her breast against a thorn and sings all night to stain a white rose red for a student. Other tales include "The Birthday of the Infanta," in which a dwarf dies of a broken heart and the Infanta demands that playmates have no hearts, and "The Remarkable Rocket," about a conceited firework that cries and fails to go off.
